screens.title: Introduction to the SDLC
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll meet the Software Development Life Cycle, or SDLC. The SDLC is a conceptual blueprint teams use to organize the work of building software, from an early feasibility idea through deployment and ongoing maintenance. It helps teams turn user needs into a reliable system by separating work into phases that focus on understanding, planning, building, verifying, releasing, and supporting. Think of it as an architect's set of plans: if the foundation, structure, and finish are planned and inspected, the finished house is safer and more predictable. A concrete example we'll use throughout is a simple to-do list web app: we will describe what to do in each phase — from asking users what they need, to sketching wireframes, to writing code, to testing, and then keeping the app healthy after launch. A common misconception is that SDLC is a rigid rulebook; in reality it is a framework that adapts to methods like Waterfall or Agile. By the end of these screens you'll be able to name each core phase, explain the main activities inside them, and map a small project to the SDLC so that decisions and risks are easier to manage. What matters most is using the SDLC to reduce surprises and keep quality visible.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Introduction to the SDLC
Introduction to the SDLC
A practical framework to plan, build, verify, and maintain software with fewer surprises.
This chapter helps you recognize the six generic SDLC phases, the core activities each phase covers, and how the SDLC becomes a planning tool for project quality and risk control. Expect concrete examples and a short mapping activity for a simple to-do list app to practice each phase.
Explore Key Topics
Requirements
Elicit what users need and capture functional and non-functional requirements clearly.
Design
Translate requirements into architecture, wireframes, and data models.
Testing & Maintenance
Verify correctness, plan releases, and keep the app secure and useful after launch.
In this lesson: concrete phase activities, common mistakes to avoid, and one project mapping exercise.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives set what you will be able to do with the SDLC. First, you will define the SDLC and explain its purpose: to create a repeatable roadmap that reduces risk and improves quality. For example, when you can name the six phases, you can create checkpoints to catch problems early. Second, you will list and describe the generic phases — requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment, and maintenance — and know the core activity in each one. That skill matters because each phase requires different roles and deliverables. Third, you will explain the primary purpose of each phase and the typical tasks performed there, such as writing user stories during requirements or performing integration tests during testing. Fourth, you will understand how the SDLC supports project management, quality assurance, and risk mitigation by making responsibilities and expectations visible. Together these objectives form a foundation you can apply to a small to-do list app or scale up to larger systems, and they prepare you to recognize common implementation errors and corrective strategies. As you move forward, keep these objectives in mind and try to map each screen back to one or more of these measurable skills.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Skills
screens.narratorSegment: These additional objectives focus on practical application and avoidance of common mistakes. First, you will identify common SDLC implementation mistakes, such as rushing requirements or skipping tests, and learn strategies to avoid them, like structured stakeholder interviews and planning rollback strategies. For example, when a team rushes requirements they often build the wrong feature and pay the cost later in rework. Second, you will distinguish functional requirements — what the system does — from non-functional requirements — how well it performs — and learn why capturing both matters. Third, you will apply the SDLC to a concrete small project: mapping a to-do list web app to specific SDLC activities, from user interviews to deployment checks. Fourth, you will recognize the special importance of testing in safety-critical contexts and why testing cannot be compromised in those systems. These objectives strengthen your practical readiness: not only will you know the phases, you'll be able to use them to make decisions, prioritize work, and reduce risky shortcuts that commonly cause project failure.

screens.title: What is the SDLC?
screens.narratorSegment: The SDLC is a conceptual model describing the stages needed to develop an information system from early feasibility through deployment and maintenance. At its core, it creates a predictable sequence of responsibilities and checkpoints so teams address the right questions at the right time. A useful metaphor is a house build: you gather requirements like asking how many rooms and the budget, design blueprints for structure and wiring, implement the build, test for leaks and safety, hand over to occupants, and then maintain the house over time. Concretely, for a to-do list app the SDLC means first gathering user stories that describe adding and sharing tasks, then designing a simple UI and a small database table, implementing backend endpoints and the frontend UI, testing the flows, deploying to a server, and monitoring for bugs post-launch. A common misconception is treating the SDLC as a single fixed sequence; instead, think of it as a flexible roadmap you adapt to team size, risk, and project scale. In short, the SDLC gives structure without stifling adaptation. Ask yourself: which phase of the SDLC would deliver the most value first for a minimal viable version of your project?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › What is the SDLC?
Definition
A conceptual model describing stages for development, from feasibility through maintenance.
House-building metaphor
Gather needs (rooms, budget), create blueprints, build, inspect, hand over, and maintain. The same flow helps software teams reduce surprises.
Example: To-Do List App
  • Requirements: user stories for tasks and sharing.
  • Design: wireframe input and list layout, DB table for tasks.
  • Implementation: endpoints to add, update, delete tasks.
Key Takeaway

Treat the SDLC as a guiding roadmap that makes responsibilities and risks visible without prescribing a single execution style.

Quick reference: core idea
Six phases provide checkpoints and deliverables so teams can inspect and adapt work as it progresses.
Requirements
Design
Implementation
Testing
Deployment
Maintenance
Misconception check: SDLC is not a single methodology — it is a structure that can be used with Waterfall, Agile, or other approaches.

screens.title: Requirements Gathering and Analysis
screens.narratorSegment: Requirements gathering is the foundation of a successful SDLC. It is the phase where teams learn what users need, what stakeholders expect, and what constraints exist, and then record those findings as functional and non-functional requirements. Functional requirements describe actions the system must perform, such as adding a task or sharing a list. Non-functional requirements describe qualities like security, performance, and usability — for example, the app should respond to a new task within one second on average or encrypt shared lists. Typical activities include stakeholder interviews, workshops, surveys, and writing user stories that capture value from a user's perspective. A concrete activity for the to-do list app is conducting three short interviews to collect common task behaviors and then converting them into user stories like: 'As a user, I want to add a task so I can track work.' A common mistake is rushing this phase or making assumptions without verification. That leads to expensive rework later because the team built to the wrong expectations. To avoid this, create clear acceptance criteria and validate them with a representative user. Key takeaway: invest time here to reduce later surprises. Which user story would you prioritize first for a minimum viable to-do experience?

keyIdea.title: Requirements matter most
keyIdea.text: Well-gathered functional and non-functional requirements reduce the risk of building the wrong solution.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Requirements Gathering
Phase activities
  1. Stakeholder interviews and workshops to elicit needs.
  2. Document functional and non-functional requirements.
  3. Create user stories and acceptance criteria.
  4. Validate assumptions with users or prototypes.
Concrete task
For a to-do app, run three user interviews and write five user stories such as: 'As a user, I want to add a task so I can remember items.'
Common mistakes & checks
Rushing requirements leads to rework.
Assuming user intent instead of validating it.
Mitigation: acceptance criteria and quick validation tests.
Key Takeaway

Capture both what the system does and how well it must perform; validate early with users to prevent costly rework.

screens.title: Design: Translating 'What' into 'How'
screens.narratorSegment: The design phase takes requirements and turns them into concrete plans that developers can implement. Design covers system architecture, database models, user interface sketches, and security decisions. For example, in a to-do list app a design decision is whether to store tasks in a single table keyed to user accounts, and how to represent shared lists and permissions. Another decision is whether the UI will favor an inline add-control for speed or a modal input for clarity. Security design must also be considered: will shared lists be encrypted at rest or restricted via access control? A clear design reduces integration problems later — it provides a shared language and artifacts such as architecture diagrams, wireframes, A P I contracts, and data schemas. A common misconception is that design is purely aesthetic; in fact, good design reduces technical debt, makes code easier to test, and documents expected behaviors. Practical actions in this phase include drawing wireframes, drafting A P I endpoints and request/response formats, and creating a simple ER diagram for your database. Key takeaway: make design decisions explicit and review them with developers and stakeholders to avoid late surprises. Which design decision will most reduce uncertainty for your to-do app?

keyIdea.title: Design creates the blueprint
keyIdea.text: Design produces the architecture, UI plans, data structures, and security rules that guide implementation and testing.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Design
Design deliverables
  • High-level architecture and component interactions.
  • Data model or database schema.
  • UI wireframes and UX flow maps.
  • Security and performance constraints.
Concrete design task
Sketch a wireframe for the task entry and list display, and design a simple tasks table with fields for id, user_id, text, completed, and shared_with.
Design tradeoffs
Simplicity vs extensibility: simple schema first, extend later with migrations.
Performance vs consistency: caching can help but adds complexity.
Security vs convenience: permissions and encryption increase safety but require planning.
Key Takeaway

Document design decisions clearly; they become a contract between product, design, and engineering and reduce later integration rework.

screens.title: Implementation: Writing the Code
screens.narratorSegment: Implementation is where designs become real software. Developers write code, create modules, and build APIs and user interfaces following the design documents. Implementation commonly includes unit testing by developers and code reviews to catch defects early and enforce standards. For a to-do list app a typical implementation step is creating an endpoint to add a task, writing a small function that inserts a row into the tasks table, and adding a unit test that verifies a task appears when the A P I is called. Code reviews help prevent unstructured, fragile code often called 'spaghetti code' and keep style consistent. A frequent misconception is that implementation is only typing code; in reality it includes automated tests, instrumentation, and documentation. Practical practices include writing small, testable functions, running unit tests automatically, and using pull requests for review. Example: write one unit test that creates a task and asserts it exists, then a second test that marks a task complete. Closing question: after implementation, what small test would you add first to validate your to-do app's most important behavior? Implementation: Writing the Code means implementation must include coding, unit tests, and peer review to ensure quality and maintainability.. In practical terms, translate design into working software with testing and code review. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Implementation must include coding, unit tests, and peer review to ensure quality and maintainability.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Implementation
Developer activities
  • Write modules and endpoints that implement the design.
  • Create unit tests for individual functions.
  • Conduct code reviews and adhere to coding standards.
  • Document API contracts and deployment notes.
Concrete example
Create a unit test that posts a new task and checks the data store for the created record. Add a second test that marks it complete and asserts status changed.
Code snippet (visual)
# Pseudo-code illustration post('/tasks') -> insert task into tasks table unit_test: create task -> assert found unit_test: mark complete -> assert completed == true
Misconception: tests are optional. In practice, tests are part of implementation and reduce regression risk when making changes.
Key Takeaway

Implement with small testable units and require peer reviews so code remains robust and maintainable.

screens.title: Testing: Verify, Validate, and Protect
screens.narratorSegment: Testing is the phase where the team verifies that the implementation meets requirements and uncovers defects before release. It includes unit, integration, system, user acceptance, performance, and security testing. Unit tests confirm small components behave correctly in isolation. Integration tests ensure modules work together — for example, that the task creation endpoint updates the database and that the UI reflects the change. System testing validates the complete application against requirements. User acceptance testing involves real users verifying the software satisfies business needs. Performance and security testing assess non-functional requirements like responsiveness under load and vulnerability to attack. In safety-critical systems, testing is especially rigorous because defects can cause harm. A common mistake is running only a subset of tests or relying on manual checks; automated test suites and clear test plans help avoid that. Practical example: for the to-do app, write integration tests that simulate a user adding, editing, and sharing tasks, and include a performance check for 100 concurrent users if scaling matters. Final question: which test type would catch a broken permission check when sharing lists? Testing: Verify, Validate, and Protect means multiple testing types ensure correctness at different scopes: unit, integration, system, acceptance, performance, and security.. In practical terms, types of testing and why each is necessary. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Multiple testing types ensure correctness at different scopes: unit, integration, system, acceptance, performance, and security.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Testing
Types of testing
  • Unit testing: components in isolation.
  • Integration testing: components working together.
  • System testing: the full application against requirements.
  • User acceptance testing: validation by real users.
  • Performance and security testing for non-functional needs.
Concrete test
Integration test: call the add-task API, confirm DB entry, and load the UI to confirm the task appears. That sequence catches cross-layer bugs.
Risks and mitigations
Skipping tests risks production defects and security issues.
Mitigation: automated suites and clear test plans.
Critical systems need exhaustive verification and traceable evidence of tests.
Key Takeaway

Testing should be layered and planned; automate where possible and never shortcut tests for high-risk systems.

screens.title: Deployment: Releasing with Confidence
screens.narratorSegment: Deployment is the process of making the tested software available in production. It involves release planning, environment configuration, installation, and often user training. For example, a deployment plan for the to-do list app might schedule a low-traffic window, provision a production database, migrate the schema, and run smoke tests to ensure basic flows work. A crucial activity is planning rollback strategies: if an issue appears, how will you return to the previous stable version with minimal downtime? Another common responsibility is environment parity — ensuring staging closely mirrors production so tests are meaningful. A frequent mistake is insufficient deployment planning or no rollback path, which can cause extended outages. Mitigation strategies include blue-green or canary deployments when possible, database migration backups, and clear communication with stakeholders about the release window. Final thought: deployment isn't a single moment; it is a planned sequence of steps and checks. After deployment, monitoring and maintenance activities keep the app healthy. What rollback plan would you prepare for a small web app release? Deployment: Releasing with Confidence means deployment requires careful planning, environment setup, rollback strategies, and post-release checks to protect users and services.. In practical terms, plans, environments, rollbacks, and user training. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Deployment requires careful planning, environment setup, rollback strategies, and post-release checks to protect users and services.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Deployment
Deployment checklist
  • Release planning and schedule.
  • Environment setup and configuration.
  • Database migration and backups.
  • Smoke tests and verification steps.
Concrete plan
For the to-do app: deploy in low-traffic window, run migration with backup, run smoke tests that add and list a task, and monitor logs for errors for the first hour.
Rollback & mitigation
No rollback strategy risks prolonged outages.
Mitigation: keep database backups and use blue-green or canary releases as available.
Communicate release windows and user impact clearly to stakeholders.
Key Takeaway

Treat deployment as a planned operation with checks and rollback paths, not an afterthought.

screens.title: Maintenance: The Ongoing Phase
screens.narratorSegment: Maintenance is the long-running phase after deployment where the software is kept useful, secure, and performant. It includes fixing bugs found in production, delivering enhancements and new features based on user feedback, optimizing performance, and applying security updates and patches. For a small to-do list app maintenance tasks might include fixing a bug that causes tasks to disappear on refresh, adding a requested due-date field, improving query performance, or patching a vulnerability in a shared-list feature. Maintenance can dominate the cost of ownership if neglected; systems that are not actively maintained become insecure, slow, and unusable. A common misconception is that maintenance is only reactive; the best teams operate proactively, scheduling refactors, performance tuning, and regular security updates. Practical maintenance disciplines include tracking defects with a ticketing system, prioritizing issues against user impact, and scheduling periodic reviews. screens.title: Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
screens.narratorSegment: Across SDLC phases there are recurring mistakes that increase cost and risk. One of the most damaging is rushing requirements: teams that skip interviews and assume needs often deliver the wrong product. Another frequent error is inadequate testing or skipping automated tests, which allows regressions and security flaws to reach production. Poor design discipline, such as unclear interfaces or undocumented data structures, causes integration friction and rework. Deployment without rollback plans or environment parity creates outages. Finally, neglecting maintenance lets defects accumulate and reduces long-term value. For each mistake there are practical mitigations: spend effort validating requirements with short user interviews and prototypes; enforce unit and integration tests with automated pipelines; record design decisions in simple diagrams and A P I contracts; plan deployments with backups and smoke tests; and schedule regular maintenance cycles and monitoring. The to-do list example shows each mitigation: validate the add-task flow with users, add automated tests, document the A P I contract, and plan a quick rollback in case of an incident. Question for reflection: which mitigation would most reduce risk on your next small project?

screens.title: SDLC and Development Methodologies
screens.narratorSegment: It is important to distinguish the SDLC, which is a conceptual lifecycle, from specific development methodologies like Waterfall or Agile. The SDLC names the phases any project must handle: requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment, and maintenance. Waterfall maps those phases sequentially, often completing one before starting the next, which can suit projects with stable requirements but risks late discovery of problems. Agile and Scrum apply the SDLC iteratively: teams plan small increments that cycle through many SDLC phases quickly, allowing feedback and adaptation. For a small to-do app, an iterative approach might deliver a minimal add-and-list feature first, gather feedback, then iterate with design and implementation of sharing. A common misconception is to equate SDLC to Waterfall; in reality SDLC underlies many methodological choices. The core insight is that the SDLC guides what needs to be addressed; the methodology decides how to schedule and iterate those activities. Which approach would help you get usable feedback fastest for a new feature? fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll meet the Software Development Life Cycle, or SDLC. The SDLC is a conceptual blueprint teams use to organize the work of building software, from an early feasibility idea through deployment and ongoing maintenance. It helps teams turn user needs into a reliable system by separating work into phases that focus on understanding, planning, building, verifying, releasing, and supporting. Think of it as an architect's set of plans: if the foundation, structure, and finish are planned and inspected, the finished house is safer and more predictable. A concrete example we'll use throughout is a simple to-do list web app: we will describe what to do in each phase — from asking users what they need, to sketching wireframes, to writing code, to testing, and then keeping the app healthy after launch. A common misconception is that SDLC is a rigid rulebook; in reality it is a framework that adapts to methods like Waterfall or Agile. By the end of these screens you'll be able to name each core phase, explain the main activities inside them, and map a small project to the SDLC so that decisions and risks are easier to manage. What matters most is using the SDLC to reduce surprises and keep quality visible.

These learning objectives set what you will be able to do with the SDLC. First, you will define the SDLC and explain its purpose: to create a repeatable roadmap that reduces risk and improves quality. For example, when you can name the six phases, you can create checkpoints to catch problems early. Second, you will list and describe the generic phases — requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment, and maintenance — and know the core activity in each one. That skill matters because each phase requires different roles and deliverables. Third, you will explain the primary purpose of each phase and the typical tasks performed there, such as writing user stories during requirements or performing integration tests during testing. Fourth, you will understand how the SDLC supports project management, quality assurance, and risk mitigation by making responsibilities and expectations visible. Together these objectives form a foundation you can apply to a small to-do list app or scale up to larger systems, and they prepare you to recognize common implementation errors and corrective strategies. As you move forward, keep these objectives in mind and try to map each screen back to one or more of these measurable skills.

These additional objectives focus on practical application and avoidance of common mistakes. First, you will identify common SDLC implementation mistakes, such as rushing requirements or skipping tests, and learn strategies to avoid them, like structured stakeholder interviews and planning rollback strategies. For example, when a team rushes requirements they often build the wrong feature and pay the cost later in rework. Second, you will distinguish functional requirements — what the system does — from non-functional requirements — how well it performs — and learn why capturing both matters. Third, you will apply the SDLC to a concrete small project: mapping a to-do list web app to specific SDLC activities, from user interviews to deployment checks. Fourth, you will recognize the special importance of testing in safety-critical contexts and why testing cannot be compromised in those systems. These objectives strengthen your practical readiness: not only will you know the phases, you'll be able to use them to make decisions, prioritize work, and reduce risky shortcuts that commonly cause project failure.

The SDLC is a conceptual model describing the stages needed to develop an information system from early feasibility through deployment and maintenance. At its core, it creates a predictable sequence of responsibilities and checkpoints so teams address the right questions at the right time. A useful metaphor is a house build: you gather requirements like asking how many rooms and the budget, design blueprints for structure and wiring, implement the build, test for leaks and safety, hand over to occupants, and then maintain the house over time. Concretely, for a to-do list app the SDLC means first gathering user stories that describe adding and sharing tasks, then designing a simple UI and a small database table, implementing backend endpoints and the frontend UI, testing the flows, deploying to a server, and monitoring for bugs post-launch. A common misconception is treating the SDLC as a single fixed sequence; instead, think of it as a flexible roadmap you adapt to team size, risk, and project scale. In short, the SDLC gives structure without stifling adaptation. Ask yourself: which phase of the SDLC would deliver the most value first for a minimal viable version of your project?

Requirements gathering is the foundation of a successful SDLC. It is the phase where teams learn what users need, what stakeholders expect, and what constraints exist, and then record those findings as functional and non-functional requirements. Functional requirements describe actions the system must perform, such as adding a task or sharing a list. Non-functional requirements describe qualities like security, performance, and usability — for example, the app should respond to a new task within one second on average or encrypt shared lists. Typical activities include stakeholder interviews, workshops, surveys, and writing user stories that capture value from a user's perspective. A concrete activity for the to-do list app is conducting three short interviews to collect common task behaviors and then converting them into user stories like: 'As a user, I want to add a task so I can track work.' A common mistake is rushing this phase or making assumptions without verification. That leads to expensive rework later because the team built to the wrong expectations. To avoid this, create clear acceptance criteria and validate them with a representative user. Key takeaway: invest time here to reduce later surprises. Which user story would you prioritize first for a minimum viable to-do experience?

The design phase takes requirements and turns them into concrete plans that developers can implement. Design covers system architecture, database models, user interface sketches, and security decisions. For example, in a to-do list app a design decision is whether to store tasks in a single table keyed to user accounts, and how to represent shared lists and permissions. Another decision is whether the UI will favor an inline add-control for speed or a modal input for clarity. Security design must also be considered: will shared lists be encrypted at rest or restricted via access control? A clear design reduces integration problems later — it provides a shared language and artifacts such as architecture diagrams, wireframes, A P I contracts, and data schemas. A common misconception is that design is purely aesthetic; in fact, good design reduces technical debt, makes code easier to test, and documents expected behaviors. Practical actions in this phase include drawing wireframes, drafting A P I endpoints and request/response formats, and creating a simple ER diagram for your database. Key takeaway: make design decisions explicit and review them with developers and stakeholders to avoid late surprises. Which design decision will most reduce uncertainty for your to-do app?

Implementation is where designs become real software. Developers write code, create modules, and build APIs and user interfaces following the design documents. Implementation commonly includes unit testing by developers and code reviews to catch defects early and enforce standards. For a to-do list app a typical implementation step is creating an endpoint to add a task, writing a small function that inserts a row into the tasks table, and adding a unit test that verifies a task appears when the A P I is called. Code reviews help prevent unstructured, fragile code often called 'spaghetti code' and keep style consistent. A frequent misconception is that implementation is only typing code; in reality it includes automated tests, instrumentation, and documentation. Practical practices include writing small, testable functions, running unit tests automatically, and using pull requests for review. Example: write one unit test that creates a task and asserts it exists, then a second test that marks a task complete. Closing question: after implementation, what small test would you add first to validate your to-do app's most important behavior? Implementation: Writing the Code means implementation must include coding, unit tests, and peer review to ensure quality and maintainability.. In practical terms, translate design into working software with testing and code review. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Testing is the phase where the team verifies that the implementation meets requirements and uncovers defects before release. It includes unit, integration, system, user acceptance, performance, and security testing. Unit tests confirm small components behave correctly in isolation. Integration tests ensure modules work together — for example, that the task creation endpoint updates the database and that the UI reflects the change. System testing validates the complete application against requirements. User acceptance testing involves real users verifying the software satisfies business needs. Performance and security testing assess non-functional requirements like responsiveness under load and vulnerability to attack. In safety-critical systems, testing is especially rigorous because defects can cause harm. A common mistake is running only a subset of tests or relying on manual checks; automated test suites and clear test plans help avoid that. Practical example: for the to-do app, write integration tests that simulate a user adding, editing, and sharing tasks, and include a performance check for 100 concurrent users if scaling matters. Final question: which test type would catch a broken permission check when sharing lists? Testing: Verify, Validate, and Protect means multiple testing types ensure correctness at different scopes: unit, integration, system, acceptance, performance, and security.. Deployment is the process of making the tested software available in production. It involves release planning, environment configuration, installation, and often user training. For example, a deployment plan for the to-do list app might schedule a low-traffic window, provision a production database, migrate the schema, and run smoke tests to ensure basic flows work. A crucial activity is planning rollback strategies: if an issue appears, how will you return to the previous stable version with minimal downtime? Another common responsibility is environment parity — ensuring staging closely mirrors production so tests are meaningful. A frequent mistake is insufficient deployment planning or no rollback path, which can cause extended outages. Mitigation strategies include blue-green or canary deployments when possible, database migration backups, and clear communication with stakeholders about the release window. Final thought: deployment isn't a single moment; it is a planned sequence of steps and checks. After deployment, monitoring and maintenance activities keep the app healthy. It includes fixing bugs found in production, delivering enhancements and new features based on user feedback, optimizing performance, and applying security updates and patches. It is important to distinguish the SDLC, which is a conceptual lifecycle, from specific development methodologies like Waterfall or Agile. The SDLC names the phases any project must handle: requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment, and maintenance. Waterfall maps those phases sequentially, often completing one before starting the next, which can suit projects with stable requirements but risks late discovery of problems. Agile and Scrum apply the SDLC iteratively: teams plan small increments that cycle through many SDLC phases quickly, allowing feedback and adaptation. For a small to-do app, an iterative approach might deliver a minimal add-and-list feature first, gather feedback, then iterate with design and implementation of sharing. A common misconception is to equate SDLC to Waterfall; in reality SDLC underlies many methodological choices. The core insight is that the SDLC guides what needs to be addressed; the methodology decides how to schedule and iterate those activities. Let's pull together the essential ideas to remember. First: the SDLC is a framework describing the lifecycle stages of software: requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment, and maintenance. It is a roadmap that makes responsibilities and quality checks visible. Second: requirements are critical — clearly capture functional and non-functional requirements and validate them early to avoid building the wrong product. Third: testing and maintenance are not optional; layered testing prevents defects, and ongoing maintenance sustains value, performance, and security after deployment. These three ideas form the backbone of disciplined software development. When you plan a small project, write clear acceptance criteria, add tests as you code, and include a maintenance plan before you release.
